choices.en: Thank you! How are you?
Thanks! How is your morning?
Thank you! Is this Maple Street?
choices.pt: Obrigado! Esta é a Maple Street?

1.reading_talk2: What changed between the first text and the new situation? Give one detail from each.

board_tasks.4: Greet a neighbor who is in a hurry. Say goodbye without starting a long conversation.
board_tasks.7: You used Good night when you arrived. Repair the greeting.
board_tasks.11: Ask your partner how they are, then respond to the answer.
board_tasks.14: Your partner did not hear your name. Say it again clearly.

reading_text: Every country has its own way to say hello. In the UK and the USA, people usually say "Hello" or "Hi" and shake hands. They also ask, "How are you?" but they do not expect a long answer. You just say, "I'm fine, thanks. And you?"
In Japan, people bow. The bow can be short for friends and deep for a boss or a teacher. In Brazil, friends often kiss on the cheek. In India, many people put their hands together and say "Namaste".
A smile is the same everywhere. So when you don't know what to do, smile and say "Hello!"

Later, Mia sees Ken again by the gate. This time he is carrying a heavy bag and looking at his watch. She says hello and asks whether he needs help. Ken thanks her, but his bus has arrived. Mia smiles and lets him go. In the evening, they meet with more time to talk. The same greeting can begin either a short exchange or a longer conversation. The listener’s situation helps Mia choose what to say next.

2.reading_talk2: What changed between the first text and the new situation? Give one detail from each.

board_tasks.4: Introduce a classmate using the name they prefer.
board_tasks.7: You said the name incorrectly. Ask how to say it.
board_tasks.11: Ask for a name and repeat it to check.
board_tasks.14: Your partner forgot your name. Reintroduce yourself kindly.

reading_text: In English, a name has two parts. The first name comes first: Anna. The last name comes second: Smith. Together they make your full name: Anna Smith.

Many people have a nickname. A nickname is a short or friendly name. Robert is Bob. Elizabeth is Liz. William is Bill. Your friends call you by your nickname, but your teacher usually uses your first name.
When you meet someone, say: "Hello, I'm Anna. Nice to meet you." Then ask: "What's your name?"

At the community desk, Tom writes a visitor badge for Ana. Her form says Ana Maria, but she wants Ana on the badge. Tom asks before he writes. He reads the letters back, and Ana notices that he has added an extra n. Tom corrects it and shows her the new badge. Ana smiles. A name may look like a small detail on a form, but checking it shows respect for the person who will wear it.

choices.pt: Sério? Que legal! Onde você mora agora?

3.reading_talk2: What changed between the first text and the new situation? Give one detail from each.

board_tasks.4: Ask where a neighbor is from without guessing.
board_tasks.7: You guessed a country from someone’s appearance. Repair your question.
board_tasks.11: Say where you live now and ask about your partner.
board_tasks.14: Your partner names a place you do not know. Ask one follow-up question.

reading_text: Maple Street is a small street with big dreams. Mia is from Brazil. She is a teacher. Ken is from Japan and he is a chef. Sara is from Egypt. She is a nurse. Tom is from England and he is a driver.
They speak different languages. Mia speaks Portuguese, Ken speaks Japanese, Sara speaks Arabic and Tom speaks English. But in the street, everybody speaks English together.
Every Friday there is a street party. People bring food from their countries. There is feijoada from Brazil, sushi from Japan, koshari from Egypt and fish and chips from England!

At the welcome table, Sara puts a map beside the food. Each neighbor points to a place that matters to them. Tom is from England, but he has lived in other countries too. A child guesses that Ken speaks Chinese. Ken gently says that he speaks Japanese. Sara asks everyone to listen to each person’s answer instead of guessing from a face or a name. Soon the map has several colored pins, and every pin has a different story.

4.reading_talk2: What changed between the first text and the new situation? Give one detail from each.

board_tasks.4: Order fruit using two different quantities.
board_tasks.7: You counted seven instead of eight oranges. Check again aloud.
board_tasks.11: Ask the price and confirm the total.
board_tasks.14: You received the wrong change. Ask politely for a check.

reading_text: Leo has a stall at the market on Maple Street. He sells fruit and bread. Every morning he counts his fruit. He has ten red apples, twelve yellow bananas and fifteen oranges.
Ana comes to the stall at nine o'clock. She wants six apples and eight oranges. Leo counts the fruit: six apples, eight oranges. That's fourteen fruits.
The apples are two dollars and the oranges are three dollars. Ana pays twenty dollars. Leo gives her six dollars back. "Thank you!" says Ana.

Ana buys fruit for a class party. She needs six apples and eight oranges. Leo puts the fruit in two separate bags and counts aloud with her. At first there are only seven oranges; one is behind the basket. They find it and count again. Ana writes both numbers on her list so that she can explain the order to the teacher. Before leaving, she checks the receipt and the bags. Counting together prevents a small mistake from becoming a problem later.

choices.en: How do you spell that?
Could you spell that slowly, please?
Can you repeat the letters?

5.reading_talk2: What changed between the first text and the new situation? Give one detail from each.

board_tasks.4: Ask someone to spell their name slowly.
board_tasks.7: You wrote one letter incorrectly. Ask for repetition.
board_tasks.11: Spell a name and have a partner read it back.
board_tasks.14: An email address has a wrong letter. Point it out politely.

reading_text: Hana is new in town. On Monday she goes to the library on Maple Street. She wants a library card. The librarian, Emma, asks for her name and her email address.
Hana spells her name: H-A-N-A. Her last name is Kim: K-I-M. Her email is hana dot kim at mail dot com. Emma writes everything on a form.
Then Emma gives her a blue card. "You can borrow three books for two weeks," says Emma. Hana chooses a book about animals and says, "Thank you very much!"

The library is busy when Hana asks for a card. Emma hears Hana’s name but cannot hear the last letter clearly. Hana spells it slowly. Emma types the email address, then points to each part of it on the screen. One letter is wrong. Hana asks Emma to change it, and they read the address together once more. Now a message about her borrowed books can reach her. Spelling is a practical way to solve a misunderstanding, not just a classroom exercise.

choices.en: Oh, sorry! Excuse me, Mia.
Sorry, Mia. Are you all right?
Excuse me, Mia. May I pass?

6.reading_talk2: What changed between the first text and the new situation? Give one detail from each.

board_tasks.4: Make a request with please and respond to thank you.
board_tasks.7: You stepped into the line by mistake. Apologize and move.
board_tasks.11: Ask to pass someone in a crowded bakery.
board_tasks.14: Your order is wrong. Explain the problem politely.

reading_text: Omar's bakery on Maple Street opens at six. At seven there is a long line outside. Everybody is polite. A woman says, "Good morning! A coffee and a bread roll, please." Omar answers, "Here you are." "Thank you very much!" "You're welcome!"
A boy bumps into a man in the line. "Oh, sorry!" says the boy. "No problem," says the man. A girl wants to pass: "Excuse me, please." Everybody makes space.
Omar smiles. "Polite words are free," he says, "but they make everybody happy." On the wall there is a sign: PLEASE and THANK YOU are always welcome here.

The bakery is crowded before work. Someone steps in front of Lena without seeing the line. He notices, says sorry, and moves behind her. When Lena reaches the counter, she asks Omar for a coffee and bread, please. Omar repeats the order before giving her a bag. Outside, another person holds the door open, and Lena thanks them. Three short expressions help people handle a busy morning kindly: excuse me, sorry, and thank you.

board_tasks.4: Identify one near object and one far object.
board_tasks.7: You pointed to the wrong book. Clarify which one you mean.
board_tasks.11: Ask a partner about an object across the room.
board_tasks.14: Your partner says this but points far away. Ask for clarification.

reading_text: Mia's classroom is on the first floor. There is a big board on the wall and a clock above the door. There are twelve desks, twelve chairs and four windows.

On Mia's desk there are books, pens and pencils. Zoe has a green bag. Paul has a blue bag. "What's this?" asks Zoe, pointing at a small box. "It's a pencil case," says Mia. "And what's that?" asks Paul, pointing at the clock. "That's a clock. It's nine o'clock. Time for class!"
The students sit down and open their notebooks. Mia writes a word on the board: WELCOME.

Zoe cannot find her blue notebook. She points to a blue object on the shelf across the room and asks Paul whether that is hers. Paul checks: it is a dictionary. Then he points to a notebook on the desk beside Zoe and asks whether this one is hers. Zoe laughs. Her notebook was close to her all along. Their gestures matter because the words this and that depend on where the objects are in relation to the speaker.

board_tasks.11: Ask whether the shop has the toy in another color.
board_tasks.14: The seller brings the wrong color. Correct the request kindly.

reading_text: Rosa has a toy shop with colorful things. In the window there is a red car, a blue ball and a green frog. On the shelf there is a yellow duck, a white rabbit and a black cat.
A boy named Ben comes in with his mother. "What's your favorite color?" asks Rosa. "Blue!" says Ben. Rosa gives him the blue ball. "It's a present," she says. Ben is very happy.
Lily loves purple. She chooses a purple teddy bear. "My favorite color is purple, too," says Rosa. Now Lily has a purple bear and a big smile.

Ben sees two blue toys in Rosa’s shop window: a car and a ball. He tells Rosa that he wants the blue one. She picks up the car, but Ben means the ball. He says the color and the object together, and Rosa finds the right gift. Lily has a similar problem with two bears. She points to the purple bear before Rosa takes it down. A color helps, but naming the object as well makes the choice clear.

9.reading_talk2: What changed between the first text and the new situation? Give one detail from each.

board_tasks.4: Introduce two relatives using their names and relationships.
board_tasks.7: Your partner assumes everyone in the photo lives together. Clarify.
board_tasks.11: Ask a question about a family photo.
board_tasks.14: You cannot tell who is the brother. Ask a follow-up question.

reading_text: On the wall of Sara's living room there is a big family photo. In the middle there are her grandmother and grandfather. They are smiling. Next to them are her mother and father. Her mother's name is Nadia and her father's name is Karim.
In front there are Sara, her brother and her two sisters. "This is my family," says Sara to a visitor. "It's a big family, but we are very close."
Every Sunday the family has lunch together. Grandma cooks and Grandpa tells stories. The children help and the parents talk. Sara loves Sundays.

Sara shows Max a photograph of her family. She names her grandparents, parents, brother, and two sisters. Max asks whether everyone in the picture lives in her house. Sara explains that her grandmother lives in another town and her grandfather lives nearby. They meet for lunch on Sundays, but they do not share one address. The photograph records a moment together; it does not tell the whole story of where each person lives.

10.reading_talk2: What changed between the first text and the new situation? Give one detail from each.

board_tasks.4: Welcome a visitor, introduce someone, and close the exchange.
board_tasks.7: You used Good night when the party began. Repair it.
board_tasks.11: Ask one question that keeps the conversation going.
board_tasks.14: Your new friend is leaving. Suggest meeting again.

reading_text: Today is a big day on Maple Street. There is a party in the middle of the street. Mia, Ken, Sara and Tom are there. They bring food from their countries: feijoada from Brazil, sushi from Japan, koshari from Egypt and fish and chips from England.
Children play with red and blue balls. Tom plays the guitar. There are twenty chairs and fifteen tables. Everybody says "Hello!" and "Nice to meet you!"
At night, everybody says, "Good night!" and "See you next week!" Nobody wants to go home. It is the best party on the street.

At the street party, Sara welcomes a visitor and asks for her name. Ken tells the visitor where he is from. A child asks Ken to spell his name, while Tom offers the visitor a chair. She chooses the green one because it is close to the food table. Before the music starts, Sara introduces her to two more neighbors. At the end of the evening, the visitor thanks everyone and says goodbye. Small choices in language helped her join the group.
